items.stem: An adolescent reports painful menses since menarche that began about a year ago, with no abnormal bleeding between periods and a normal pelvic exam. Which pattern do these findings support?
items.rationale_correct: Painful menses beginning near menarche without pelvic pathology is primary dysmenorrhea, which is prostaglandin-mediated and responds to NSAIDs. Principle: onset near menarche plus a normal exam points to primary, not secondary, dysmenorrhea.

rationale_distractors.Secondary dysmenorrhea from endometriosi: Right when pain starts years later or with an abnormal exam.
rationale_distractors.Pelvic inflammatory disease: Right with fever, discharge, and cervical motion tenderness.
rationale_distractors.Uterine fibroids: Right with heavy bleeding and an enlarged, irregular uterus.

items.stem: A patient with primary dysmenorrhea asks how to reduce her cramps. Which first-line measure is most appropriate to teach?
options: Take an NSAID at the onset of menses as directed
Avoid all physical activity during menses
key: Take an NSAID at the onset of menses as directed
items.rationale_correct: NSAIDs reduce prostaglandin-mediated cramping and are first-line for primary dysmenorrhea. Principle: block the prostaglandin driver early for best relief.

rationale_distractors.Use opioids routinely for cramps: Not first-line and carries dependence risk.
rationale_distractors.Avoid all physical activity: Activity can help; strict rest is not advised.
rationale_distractors.Restrict fluids during menses: Not evidence-based and may worsen discomfort.

items.stem: A 51-year-old reports hot flashes, night sweats, and irregular periods for the past year. Which term best describes these vasomotor findings?
options: Vasomotor symptoms of the menopause transition
key: Vasomotor symptoms of the menopause transition
items.rationale_correct: Hot flashes and night sweats are vasomotor symptoms typical of the menopause transition. Principle: name vasomotor symptoms distinctly from genitourinary changes, which are treated differently.

rationale_distractors.Genitourinary syndrome of menopause: Right for vaginal dryness, dyspareunia, and urinary symptoms.
rationale_distractors.Primary ovarian insufficiency: Right when ovarian failure occurs before age 40.
rationale_distractors.Abnormal uterine bleeding requiring biop: Right for postmenopausal bleeding, which this is not.

items.stem: A postmenopausal patient (last menses 3 years ago) reports new vaginal bleeding. Which nursing interpretation is most appropriate?
options: This is a normal return of menses
This requires evaluation to exclude endometrial cancer
This is expected with hormone therapy and needs no follow-up
This is caused by vasomotor symptoms
key: This requires evaluation to exclude endometrial cancer
items.rationale_correct: Any postmenopausal bleeding requires endometrial evaluation to rule out cancer. Principle: postmenopausal bleeding is cancer until proven otherwise.

rationale_distractors.This is a normal return of menses: Menses do not resume years after menopause.
rationale_distractors.This is expected with hormone therapy an: Even on therapy, new bleeding is investigated.
rationale_distractors.This is caused by vasomotor symptoms: Vasomotor symptoms do not cause bleeding.

items.stem: For each patient, indicate whether a combined estrogen-progestin pill is generally Appropriate or Generally avoided based on U.S. MEC principles.

rows: Patient with history of deep vein thrombosis

items.rationale_correct: Estrogen raises thrombotic risk, so combined pills are avoided with older-plus-smoking, prior VTE, and migraine with aura. Principle: screen for estrogen contraindications before recommending a combined method.

rationale_distractors.(estrogen-contraindicated rows): Each avoided row would still allow a progestin-only or non-hormonal method — the contraindication is to estrogen, not to all contraception.

items.stem: A patient wants the most effective reversible contraception and prefers not to take a daily pill. Which option best matches her stated preference?
options: A long-acting reversible method such as an IUD or implant
key: A long-acting reversible method such as an IUD or implant
items.rationale_correct: LARC methods are the most effective reversible options and require no daily action, matching her preference. Principle: align the method to effectiveness plus the patient's adherence preferences.

rationale_distractors.Combined oral contraceptive pills: Effective but require daily adherence she wants to avoid.
rationale_distractors.Fertility awareness-based methods: Higher typical-use failure and demanding to follow.

items.stem: Using the ACHES mnemonic, select all warning signs the nurse teaches a patient starting a combined (estrogen-containing) oral contraceptive to report.
options: Eye problems such as vision loss
key: Eye problems such as vision loss
items.rationale_correct: ACHES flags estrogen-related thrombotic and vascular emergencies: abdominal pain, chest pain, headache, eye problems, severe leg pain. Principle: teach the danger-sign mnemonic so patients recognize a clot early.

rationale_distractors.Mild breast tenderness: A common, benign early side effect, not an ACHES warning sign.

items.stem: A patient is planning pregnancy in 6 months. Select the 3 preconception recommendations best supported by evidence.
items.rationale_correct: Preconception care centers on folic acid, medication review for teratogens, and vaccine updates. Principle: the highest-yield preconception actions reduce risk before organogenesis begins.

rationale_distractors.Start prenatal magnesium sulfate now: Magnesium is for seizure prophylaxis in preeclampsia with severe features, not preconception.
rationale_distractors.Begin low-dose aspirin for everyone: Aspirin prophylaxis is targeted to high-risk patients, not universal.

items.stem: A patient planning pregnancy has no history of neural tube defects. What daily folic acid intake does the nurse recommend before conception?
options: At least 0.4 mg (400 mcg) of folic acid daily
4 mg only after a positive pregnancy test
Folic acid is unsafe before pregnancy
key: At least 0.4 mg (400 mcg) of folic acid daily
items.rationale_correct: At least 400 mcg of folic acid daily before conception reduces neural tube defects; the 4 mg dose is reserved for a prior affected pregnancy. Principle: start folate before conception because the neural tube closes very early.

rationale_distractors.4 mg only after a positive pregnancy tes: Too late and the wrong dose for standard risk.

items.stem: Classify each sign of pregnancy as Presumptive, Probable, or Positive.

rows: Fetal heartbeat auscultated by the examiner
Fetal movement felt by the examiner

items.rationale_correct: Presumptive signs are subjective, probable are examiner-observed but not conclusive, and positive signs prove a fetus. Principle: only examiner-detected fetal heartbeat, movement, or ultrasound are positive.

rationale_distractors.(any misclassification): Calling a patient-reported symptom 'positive' or an examiner's fetal finding 'presumptive' reverses the certainty hierarchy.

items.stem: A patient reports amenorrhea, nausea, and breast tenderness and has a positive urine pregnancy test. Which statement about these findings is accurate?
options: They are presumptive and probable signs but not positive confirmation
key: They are presumptive and probable signs but not positive confirmation
items.rationale_correct: Symptoms are presumptive and a positive test is probable; only examiner-detected fetal heart, movement, or ultrasound is positive. Principle: a positive test raises probability but does not prove an intrauterine, viable fetus.

rationale_distractors.They positively confirm pregnancy: Requires a positive sign such as ultrasound.
rationale_distractors.They rule out ectopic pregnancy: They do not; location must be confirmed.
rationale_distractors.They indicate fetal viability: Viability requires cardiac activity on imaging.

items.stem: Complete the GTPAL. A patient has one prior birth at 39 weeks, one birth at 34 weeks, one miscarriage at 10 weeks, and is currently pregnant; all three prior children are living. Her GTPAL is G[1] T[2] P[3] A[4] L[5].
items.rationale_correct: Gravida counts all pregnancies including the current (4); Term is births at or after 37 weeks (1); Preterm is 20 to 36 6/7 weeks (1); Abortions are losses before 20 weeks (1); Living children (3). Principle: count each element against its exact gestational-age boundary.

rationale_distractors.(other options): Miscounting gravida (forgetting the current pregnancy) or placing the 34-week birth under Term instead of Preterm are the classic GTPAL errors.

items.stem: A patient is pregnant for the third time. She has twins born at 36 weeks (both living) and one miscarriage at 8 weeks. Which GTPAL is correct?
items.rationale_correct: Gravida counts pregnancies (3); the 36-week birth is preterm and twins count as one birth event for parity (P1); the miscarriage is an abortion (A1); two living children (L2). Principle: multiples count once for para but by head for living children.

rationale_distractors.G3 T1 P0 A1 L2: Wrongly counts the 36-week birth as term.
rationale_distractors.G3 T0 P2 A1 L2: Wrongly counts twins as two preterm births.
rationale_distractors.G2 T0 P1 A1 L2: Forgets to count the current pregnancy in gravida.

items.stem: Using Naegele's rule for a patient with a regular 28-day cycle and a last menstrual period of March 10, the estimated date of birth is [1], and if her cycles were irregular the nurse would rely instead on [2].
items.rationale_correct: Naegele's rule: LMP minus 3 months plus 7 days (March 10 → December 17). With irregular cycles, ultrasound dating supersedes it. Principle: Naegele assumes a 28-day cycle; imaging wins when that assumption fails.

rationale_distractors.December 3 / January 17: Result from omitting the +7 days or mis-subtracting the months.

items.stem: A patient's last menstrual period was July 5. Using Naegele's rule, which estimated date of birth should the nurse calculate?
items.rationale_correct: July 5 minus 3 months is April 5; plus 7 days is April 12. Principle: apply the subtract-three-months-then-add-seven-days steps in order.

rationale_distractors.March 28: Subtracts four months instead of three.

items.stem: At an initial prenatal visit, which finding in the history most warrants prompt follow-up and safety planning?
items.rationale_correct: Disclosure of intimate partner violence requires private assessment and safety planning; risk can rise in pregnancy. Principle: screen privately and respond to violence disclosure as a safety priority.

rationale_distractors.Occasional heartburn after meals: A common discomfort managed with teaching.

items.stem: A patient in the first trimester expresses ambivalence about the pregnancy despite having planned it. How should the nurse interpret this?
options: It indicates rejection of the pregnancy requiring referral
Ambivalence is a common, normal early psychological response
key: Ambivalence is a common, normal early psychological response
items.rationale_correct: Early ambivalence, even in planned pregnancies, is a normal adaptive task of pregnancy. Principle: normalize early ambivalence while remaining alert for persistent distress.

items.stem: Highlight the positive (diagnostic) signs of pregnancy in the note. 'Patient reports amenorrhea and nausea; examiner notes a positive pregnancy test, auscultates a fetal heartbeat, palpates fetal movement, and ultrasound visualizes the fetus.'
items.rationale_correct: Examiner-detected fetal heartbeat, fetal movement, and ultrasound visualization are positive signs. Principle: only findings the examiner attributes directly to a fetus are positive.

rationale_distractors.positive pregnancy test: A probable sign, since other conditions can raise hCG.

items.stem: Classify each prenatal test as a Screening test or a Diagnostic test.
items.rationale_correct: Screening tests estimate risk (cfDNA, quad, GCT); diagnostic tests provide a karyotype (CVS, amniocentesis). Principle: a positive screen estimates probability and is confirmed by a diagnostic test.

rationale_distractors.(any swap): Labeling cfDNA 'diagnostic' or amniocentesis 'screening' confuses risk estimation with confirmation and misguides counseling.

items.stem: A patient's cell-free DNA screen returns 'high risk' for trisomy 21. How should the nurse explain the result?
options: It confirms the fetus has Down syndrome
It is a screening result that estimates increased risk and needs diagnostic confirmation
It rules out all other chromosomal conditions
key: It is a screening result that estimates increased risk and needs diagnostic confirmation
items.rationale_correct: cfDNA is a screen; a high-risk result raises probability but requires diagnostic testing (CVS or amniocentesis) to confirm. Principle: never treat a screening result as a diagnosis.

rationale_distractors.It rules out all other chromosomal condi: cfDNA targets specific trisomies, not all conditions.
rationale_distractors.It requires immediate pregnancy terminat: Directive and premature; counseling and confirmation come first.

items.stem: At which gestational-age window is a vaginal-rectal culture for group B streptococcus collected?
items.rationale_correct: GBS screening is done at 36 0/7 to 37 6/7 weeks so results guide intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis. Principle: time GBS screening near term so the culture reflects labor-time colonization.

rationale_distractors.8 to 12 weeks: Too early to predict intrapartum status.
rationale_distractors.Only during active labor: Culture results are not available quickly enough in labor.

items.stem: A patient is offered amniocentesis for diagnostic testing. Which nursing action best supports ethical, patient-centered care?
options: Tell her she must have the test
Provide information and support her right to accept or decline
Perform the test without discussing risks
Decide for her based on her age
key: Provide information and support her right to accept or decline
items.rationale_correct: Diagnostic testing is elective; the nurse provides balanced information and supports informed, autonomous choice. Principle: informed consent means the patient may decline without coercion.

items.stem: An Rh-negative patient at 28 weeks with a negative antibody screen is being evaluated. Select the 2 nursing actions, the 1 condition being prevented, and the 2 parameters to verify before administration.

actions_options: Administer Rh(D) immune globulin as ordered
Educate about the purpose and timing of the injection
Withhold the injection because she has no symptoms

actions: Administer Rh(D) immune globulin as ordered
Educate about the purpose and timing of the injection

items.rationale_correct: Routine 28-week Rh(D) immune globulin prevents alloimmunization in an unsensitized Rh-negative patient; verify Rh-negative status and a negative antibody screen first. Principle: give anti-D before sensitization can occur, not after.

rationale_distractors.Give the rubella vaccine instead: A live vaccine deferred to postpartum, unrelated to Rh.
rationale_distractors.Blood glucose / Deep tendon reflexes: Relevant to GDM and magnesium therapy, not anti-D.

items.stem: An Rh-negative patient gives birth to an Rh-positive infant. Within what time frame should Rh(D) immune globulin be given postpartum?
options: It is not needed if she received it at 28 weeks
items.rationale_correct: Postpartum anti-D is given within 72 hours when the infant is Rh-positive, in addition to the 28-week dose. Principle: the postpartum dose covers the delivery-related fetomaternal bleed and is time-critical.

rationale_distractors.Within 2 weeks of birth: Too late; the 72-hour window is standard.
rationale_distractors.It is not needed if she received it at 2: The antenatal dose does not replace the postpartum dose.

items.stem: Reviewing a patient's prenatal record across visits, select the interpretation that should prompt further evaluation.

chart_data.visits: week 24: BP 116/72, weight +6 lb; week 28: BP 128/82, weight +9 lb; week 32: BP 140/90, weight +12 lb

options: Blood pressure and weight are trending normally
A rising blood pressure trend warrants closer evaluation
key: A rising blood pressure trend warrants closer evaluation
items.rationale_correct: A steady upward blood pressure trend across visits can signal an emerging hypertensive disorder and warrants evaluation. Principle: trend the prenatal record, not single readings, to catch developing problems early.

rationale_distractors.normal trends / decreasing fundal height: Each describes a different pattern; the recorded rising blood pressure contradicts them.

items.stem: A patient's 1-hour 50 g glucose challenge test is elevated. Which is the appropriate next step?
options: Diagnose gestational diabetes and start insulin
Proceed to the 3-hour oral glucose tolerance test
key: Proceed to the 3-hour oral glucose tolerance test
items.rationale_correct: An abnormal 1-hour screen is confirmed with the diagnostic 3-hour OGTT. Principle: a positive screen leads to a diagnostic test, not directly to treatment.

items.stem: A patient with a prepregnancy BMI in the normal range asks how much weight she should gain during a singleton pregnancy. Which range does the nurse cite from national guidance?
items.rationale_correct: Normal-BMI patients are advised to gain about 25 to 35 pounds per the IOM 2009 guidance. Principle: individualize gestational weight-gain targets by prepregnancy BMI.

rationale_distractors.11 to 20 pounds: The range for patients with obesity.
rationale_distractors.40 to 50 pounds: Exceeds recommendations for a normal-BMI singleton pregnancy.
rationale_distractors.Weight gain should be avoided: Unsafe; appropriate gain supports fetal growth.

items.stem: Select all appropriate nutrition teaching points for a pregnant patient.
options: Take the recommended folic acid daily
Avoid unpasteurized dairy and deli meats unless heated
Consume raw or undercooked eggs for protein
key: Take the recommended folic acid daily
Avoid unpasteurized dairy and deli meats unless heated
items.rationale_correct: Prenatal nutrition emphasizes folate, listeria precautions, mercury limits, and iron. Principle: prenatal food safety is as important as adequate intake.

rationale_distractors.Consume raw or undercooked eggs for prot: Raises foodborne-illness risk and is not recommended.

items.stem: A patient asks whether a medication is safe in pregnancy and points to an old 'Category C' label. How should the nurse explain current drug labeling?
options: Letter categories are still the official FDA system
The FDA replaced letter categories with narrative Pregnancy and Lactation Labeling
Category C means the drug is completely safe
All Category C drugs are contraindicated
key: The FDA replaced letter categories with narrative Pregnancy and Lactation Labeling
items.rationale_correct: The PLLR replaced the A/B/C/D/X letters with narrative risk information; letters persist only in older references. Principle: interpret current labels as narrative risk summaries, not letters.

rationale_distractors.Letter categories are still the official: They were removed by the PLLR.
rationale_distractors.Category C means the drug is completely: The letters never meant simple safety.

items.stem: Which medication class should the nurse recognize as fetotoxic and generally contraindicated in pregnancy?
items.rationale_correct: ACE inhibitors and ARBs are fetotoxic, especially in later pregnancy, and are avoided. Principle: flag renally active antihypertensives as pregnancy-contraindicated.

rationale_distractors.Acetaminophen at recommended doses: Generally considered acceptable for pain or fever.
rationale_distractors.Iron supplements: Used to treat or prevent anemia.

items.stem: For each report, indicate whether it is a Normal discomfort of pregnancy or a Warning sign requiring prompt evaluation.

rows: Mild ankle swelling at the end of the day
Severe persistent headache with visual changes

items.rationale_correct: Severe headache with visual change, bleeding, and sudden facial/hand edema are warning signs; mild dependent swelling and heartburn are normal. Principle: severity, suddenness, and location separate danger from normal discomfort.

rationale_distractors.(any swap): Calling a warning sign 'normal' risks missing preeclampsia or hemorrhage; calling normal heartburn a warning sign causes needless alarm.

items.stem: Highlight the warning signs in this triage call note that require prompt evaluation. '28 weeks, reports mild nasal congestion, a severe headache that will not go away, blurred vision, mild ankle swelling, and sudden swelling of the face and hands.'
options: severe headache that will not go away
sudden swelling of the face and hands
key: severe headache that will not go away
sudden swelling of the face and hands
items.rationale_correct: Severe persistent headache, visual change, and sudden facial/hand edema suggest preeclampsia and need urgent evaluation. Principle: cluster these signs together — they point to one dangerous diagnosis.

rationale_distractors.mild nasal congestion: A common benign discomfort (rhinitis of pregnancy).
rationale_distractors.mild ankle swelling: Normal dependent edema, unlike sudden facial/hand swelling.

items.stem: A prenatal patient calls the triage line with several complaints. Rank these reports from highest to lowest priority for the nurse to address.
items.rationale_correct: Bleeding and neurologic warning signs outrank benign discomforts; both danger signs are addressed before constipation or ligament pain. Principle: triage by threat to mother and fetus, not order of mention.

rationale_distractors.Mild constipation / round ligament twing: Both are normal discomforts, correctly ranked lowest, not urgent.

items.stem: During exercise, which symptom should the nurse teach a pregnant patient to stop and seek evaluation for?
items.rationale_correct: Bleeding or fluid leakage during exercise is a stop-and-evaluate warning sign; mild heart-rate rise and perspiration are expected. Principle: teach the specific stop-exercise danger signs.

rationale_distractors.Feeling warm: Normal with activity; overheating specifically is the concern.

items.stem: A patient in the first trimester reports nausea. Which self-care measure should the nurse suggest first?
options: Eat small, frequent, bland meals and crackers before rising
Take an antiemetic before trying any dietary change
key: Eat small, frequent, bland meals and crackers before rising
items.rationale_correct: Small, frequent, bland meals and dry crackers before rising are first-line for mild nausea of pregnancy. Principle: start with dietary and behavioral measures before medication.

rationale_distractors.Skip breakfast entirely: An empty stomach often worsens nausea.
rationale_distractors.Take an antiemetic before trying any die: Medication follows non-pharmacologic measures for mild nausea.

items.stem: A patient planning to breastfeed asks about breast care in pregnancy. Which teaching is appropriate?
options: Vigorously scrub the nipples with soap to toughen them
Wear a supportive bra and avoid harsh soaps on the nipples
Apply alcohol to the nipples daily
key: Wear a supportive bra and avoid harsh soaps on the nipples
items.rationale_correct: Gentle breast care with a supportive bra and avoiding drying agents prepares for lactation. Principle: protect skin integrity rather than 'toughening' the nipples.

rationale_distractors.Express colostrum frequently before term: Not routinely advised and can stimulate contractions.

items.stem: Complete the counseling. A patient with a prepregnancy BMI in the obese range should be counseled to gain about [1] during a singleton pregnancy, and the nurse should [2].

2: individualize the plan and avoid dieting for weight loss
recommend fasting one day per week

key.2: individualize the plan and avoid dieting for weight loss

items.rationale_correct: Patients with obesity are advised to gain about 11 to 20 pounds, with an individualized plan and no intentional weight-loss dieting in pregnancy. Principle: adjust the target to BMI while still supporting fetal growth.

rationale_distractors.25 to 35 pounds / 40 to 50 pounds: Ranges for normal-BMI or excessive gain.

items.stem: Select all appropriate teaching points for common discomforts of pregnancy.
options: For heartburn, eat smaller meals and avoid lying down right after eating
For constipation, increase fiber and fluids and stay active
For back pain, use good body mechanics and supportive footwear
For leg cramps, point the toes downward and hold
For nausea, try small frequent bland meals
key: For heartburn, eat smaller meals and avoid lying down right after eating
For constipation, increase fiber and fluids and stay active
For back pain, use good body mechanics and supportive footwear
For nausea, try small frequent bland meals
items.rationale_correct: Evidence-based comfort teaching targets each discomfort; for leg cramps, dorsiflex (toes up), not point them down. Principle: match each discomfort to its specific relief measure.

rationale_distractors.For leg cramps, point the toes downward: Plantarflexion can worsen the cramp; dorsiflexion relieves it.

items.stem: Select all components appropriately included in a comprehensive initial prenatal visit.
options: Baseline vital signs and physical assessment
key: Baseline vital signs and physical assessment
items.rationale_correct: The initial visit gathers history, baseline assessment, risk screening, and dating. Principle: the first visit establishes the risk profile that guides the rest of prenatal care.

rationale_distractors.Immediate cesarean scheduling: Not a component of a routine initial prenatal visit.

items.stem: During which phase of the menstrual cycle does ovulation typically occur in a regular 28-day cycle?
options: Ovulation does not occur in a 28-day cycle
items.rationale_correct: In a regular 28-day cycle, ovulation occurs around day 14, midway between menses and the next cycle. Principle: anchor fertility teaching to the mid-cycle ovulation point.

rationale_distractors.On day 1 with menses: Day 1 is the start of menstruation, not ovulation.
rationale_distractors.On day 28: The end of the luteal phase, not ovulation.
rationale_distractors.Ovulation does not occur in a 28-day cyc: Incorrect; the 28-day cycle is the classic ovulatory example.

items.stem: In an uncomplicated pregnancy, which prenatal visit schedule should the nurse teach as typical?
options: Every 4 weeks until 28 weeks, every 2 weeks until 36 weeks, then weekly
key: Every 4 weeks until 28 weeks, every 2 weeks until 36 weeks, then weekly
items.rationale_correct: The traditional schedule increases visit frequency as term approaches to catch late-emerging problems. Principle: surveillance intensifies as risk of late complications rises.

items.stem: A patient asks the difference between chorionic villus sampling and amniocentesis. Which statement is accurate?
options: CVS can be done earlier (about 10 to 13 weeks) than amniocentesis (15 weeks or later), and both are diagnostic
key: CVS can be done earlier (about 10 to 13 weeks) than amniocentesis (15 weeks or later), and both are diagnostic
items.rationale_correct: CVS provides an earlier diagnostic karyotype than amniocentesis; both are diagnostic, not screening. Principle: choose the diagnostic test by gestational-age timing and clinical need.

items.stem: A patient using an intrauterine device should be taught to report which set of warning signs, summarized by the PATCH mnemonic?
options: Period late, Abdominal pain, Chills/fever, Trouble or foul discharge, Heavy bleeding
key: Period late, Abdominal pain, Chills/fever, Trouble or foul discharge, Heavy bleeding
items.rationale_correct: PATCH captures IUD danger signs pointing to infection, expulsion, or perforation. Principle: teach the method-specific danger-sign mnemonic at insertion.

rationale_distractors.Only mild spotting: Common early and not a danger sign by itself.

items.stem: In the GTPAL system, which letter represents the number of pregnancies that ended before 20 weeks?
items.rationale_correct: In GTPAL, A counts losses before 20 weeks, spontaneous or induced. Principle: anchor the abortion count to the 20-week boundary.

rationale_distractors.T (Term): Counts births at or after 37 weeks.

items.stem: A patient is currently pregnant and reports: a full-term son (living), a set of twins born at 35 weeks (both living), and one elective abortion at 11 weeks. Which GTPAL is correct?
items.rationale_correct: Gravida 4 (three prior pregnancies plus current); one term birth; the twin birth is one preterm event (P1); one abortion; three living children. Principle: multiples count once for parity but individually for living children.

rationale_distractors.G4 T1 P2 A1 L3: Wrongly counts twins as two preterm births.
rationale_distractors.G3 T1 P1 A1 L3: Omits the current pregnancy from gravida.
rationale_distractors.G4 T2 P0 A1 L3: Wrongly classifies the 35-week twins as term.

items.stem: A patient's last menstrual period was January 20 with regular cycles. Using Naegele's rule, which estimated date of birth is correct?
items.rationale_correct: January 20 minus 3 months is October 20; plus 7 days is October 27. Principle: subtract three months, then add seven days, in that order.

items.stem: Which sign of pregnancy is considered positive (diagnostic)?
items.rationale_correct: Ultrasound visualization is a positive sign because it directly demonstrates a fetus. Principle: only direct fetal evidence is positive.

items.stem: The quad screen is typically performed during which gestational-age window?
items.rationale_correct: The quad screen is drawn at 15 to 22 weeks. Principle: match each screening test to its correct timing window.

rationale_distractors.6 to 10 weeks: Too early for the quad screen.

items.stem: A patient's quad screen returns 'screen positive.' Which nursing explanation is most accurate?
options: The fetus definitely has a chromosomal abnormality
The result indicates increased risk and diagnostic testing can be offered
key: The result indicates increased risk and diagnostic testing can be offered
items.rationale_correct: A positive quad screen raises risk and prompts an offer of diagnostic testing; it does not diagnose. Principle: a positive screen is a probability statement, not a verdict.

items.stem: Rh(D) immune globulin is routinely offered to an unsensitized Rh-negative patient at which point in pregnancy?
items.rationale_correct: Routine antenatal anti-D is given around 28 weeks, with an additional postpartum dose if the infant is Rh-positive. Principle: the 28-week dose prevents third-trimester sensitization.

rationale_distractors.At 12 weeks: Earlier than the routine antenatal dose.

items.stem: Select all situations in which an Rh-negative, unsensitized patient should receive Rh(D) immune globulin.
options: Within 72 hours of birth if the infant is Rh-positive
key: Within 72 hours of birth if the infant is Rh-positive
items.rationale_correct: Anti-D is indicated at 28 weeks and after any sensitizing event — loss, invasive procedure, or Rh-positive birth. Principle: any fetomaternal bleeding in an Rh-negative patient triggers anti-D.

rationale_distractors.When the patient is Rh-positive: Rh-positive patients cannot be sensitized to D and do not need anti-D.

items.stem: What does the abbreviation PLLR stand for in current FDA medication labeling?
items.rationale_correct: PLLR is the Pregnancy and Lactation Labeling Rule, the narrative labeling that replaced the letter categories. Principle: know the current labeling system by name.

items.stem: A patient at 30 weeks calls reporting several symptoms. Which report should the nurse address as the highest priority?
options: Sudden gush of watery fluid from the vagina
Mild ankle swelling in the evening
key: Sudden gush of watery fluid from the vagina
items.rationale_correct: A sudden gush of fluid suggests preterm rupture of membranes and needs immediate evaluation. Principle: possible membrane rupture before term outranks benign discomforts.

rationale_distractors.Mild lower back ache: Common in pregnancy unless it becomes rhythmic pressure.

items.stem: A pregnant patient reports constipation. Which self-care measure should the nurse recommend first?
options: Increase dietary fiber, fluids, and activity
Begin a daily stimulant laxative indefinitely
key: Increase dietary fiber, fluids, and activity
items.rationale_correct: Fiber, fluids, and activity are first-line for constipation in pregnancy. Principle: use dietary and lifestyle measures before laxatives.

rationale_distractors.Begin a daily stimulant laxative indefin: Not first-line and not for indefinite use.

items.stem: A patient in an uncomplicated pregnancy asks about exercise. Which teaching is appropriate?
options: Most patients can do about 150 minutes of moderate activity weekly unless contraindicated
All exercise should stop during pregnancy
key: Most patients can do about 150 minutes of moderate activity weekly unless contraindicated
items.rationale_correct: Moderate activity (about 150 minutes weekly) is recommended in uncomplicated pregnancy. Principle: encourage safe activity while teaching the stop-exercise warning signs.

rationale_distractors.Only bed rest is safe: Bed rest is not routinely recommended.
rationale_distractors.High-risk contact sports are encouraged: Contact and fall-risk sports are discouraged.

items.stem: A 30-year-old with well-controlled migraine WITHOUT aura and no other risk factors asks about combined oral contraceptives. Which nursing response is most appropriate?
options: Combined pills are absolutely contraindicated for any migraine
Combined pills may be an option; migraine without aura is generally less restrictive than migraine with aura
She must use only permanent sterilization
No contraception is safe for her
key: Combined pills may be an option; migraine without aura is generally less restrictive than migraine with aura
items.rationale_correct: Migraine without aura is less restrictive than migraine with aura, where estrogen is avoided due to stroke risk. Principle: the aura status, not merely 'migraine,' drives estrogen eligibility.

rationale_distractors.Combined pills are absolutely contraindi: Overstates; aura is the key discriminator.

items.stem: Which contraceptive method also serves as the most effective form of emergency contraception when placed within 5 days of unprotected intercourse?
items.rationale_correct: The copper IUD is the most effective emergency contraception and provides ongoing contraception. Principle: the copper IUD uniquely doubles as emergency and ongoing contraception.

rationale_distractors.Combined oral contraceptive pill: Not the most effective EC option.

items.stem: A patient reports following a strict vegan diet. Which nutrient deficiency should the nurse most specifically assess and counsel about in pregnancy?
items.rationale_correct: Vitamin B12 is found mainly in animal products, so a strict vegan diet risks deficiency that affects fetal neurologic development. Principle: match the deficiency risk to the dietary pattern.

rationale_distractors.Vitamin C: Abundant in plant foods, rarely deficient in vegans.
rationale_distractors.Sodium: Rarely deficient; excess is the more common concern.

items.stem: A perimenopausal patient asks about managing bothersome hot flashes. Which nursing response reflects current guidance?
options: Hormone therapy is not considered an option for symptom relief
Menopausal hormone therapy is the most effective option and is generally safest when started under age 60 or within 10 years of menopause
key: Menopausal hormone therapy is the most effective option and is generally safest when started under age 60 or within 10 years of menopause
items.rationale_correct: Hormone therapy is most effective for vasomotor symptoms and has the best benefit-risk profile when started before age 60 or within 10 years of menopause. Principle: the timing of initiation shapes the risk profile.

rationale_distractors.Hormone therapy is never appropriate at: Too absolute; it has a defined role.

items.stem: Which patient report during pregnancy should the nurse recognize as a warning sign of possible preeclampsia rather than a normal discomfort?
options: Mild swelling of the feet after standing
A severe, persistent headache with visual changes
key: A severe, persistent headache with visual changes
items.rationale_correct: A severe persistent headache with visual changes is a preeclampsia warning sign, unlike benign dependent swelling or heartburn. Principle: pair neurologic-visual symptoms with hypertensive disease.

items.stem: A nurse reviews a chart listing 'G5 T2 P1 A1 L3.' Which interpretation of this obstetric history is correct?
options: Five total pregnancies, two term births, one preterm birth, one loss before 20 weeks, three living children
key: Five total pregnancies, two term births, one preterm birth, one loss before 20 weeks, three living children
items.rationale_correct: GTPAL reads as gravida 5, term 2, preterm 1, abortions 1, living 3. Principle: read each letter against its definition rather than guessing from position.

rationale_distractors.Two current pregnancies: Gravida counts total pregnancies, not simultaneous ones.
